inline.s: Good man! The various illusory realms felt by all sentient beings all arise within the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of complete enlightenment. These illusory realms are like sky-flowers arising from the sky. Though the illusory flowers (the metaphor for the various illusory realms) pass away, the empty nature (the metaphor for the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment) is not destroyed. The illusory minds of sentient beings (feeling, thought, volition, consciousness) pass away along with the passing of the illusory realms; when both the illusory realm and the illusory mind are completely extinguished, the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment is unmoving (the self-nature returns from the consciousness-state to its fundamental state). To speak of awareness in dependence on the illusory realm and illusory mind - this awareness too is illusion. If one says there is awareness, one has not yet left illusion. For one who says there is no awareness, it is likewise, still not leaving illusion. Therefore when all these illusions are completely stilled, this is called the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment unmoving.

[The illusory mind] That is, the perceptual mind of feeling, thought, volition and consciousness within the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness); that is, the shadow of the six objects spoken of in the sutra text above.
This passage speaks of two minds: the illusory mind (the shadow of the six objects) and the Tathagata’s wondrous mind of complete enlightenment.
Q: What is “borrowing the false to cultivate the true”?
A: Using the falsely-combined body and mind of the five aggregates to cultivate and realize the true-tathata Dharma-body: break one portion of ignorance, realize one portion of Dharma-body.

“Good man! All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age should be far from all illusory, empty, false realms. Because they firmly hold a mind of distance, they also distance the mind that sees things as illusory. Distance being illusory, they also distance it. The distance from the distance being illusory, they also distance it. Reaching what there is nothing to distance, then all illusions are removed. For example, making fire by friction, the two sticks depending on one another: when the fire appears the sticks are consumed, the ashes fly and the smoke vanishes; to use illusion to cultivate within illusion is likewise. When all illusions are entirely extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation.”

Good man! All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age should be far from all illusory, empty, false realms. Because they firmly hold a thought of distance, this thought is also illusory and should likewise be distanced; distancing this mind of distance, this too is illusory and should also be distanced; distancing this distance, this too is illusory and should also be distanced; when one reaches what there is nothing to distance, then all illusions are removed. For example, making fire by friction: a stick quickly rubbed on a block; when the fire comes out, the stick and the block are consumed by the fire, and the ashes fly and the smoke vanishes. To use illusion to cultivate within illusion is likewise (this says: by the illusory mind to still the illusory realm; when the illusory realm is stilled, the illusory mind too is stilled). When all illusions (the illusory realm and the illusory mind) are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation (because the wondrous mind of complete enlightenment remains; the verse below says:
“Empty space is originally unmoving; illusion arises from awareness; when illusion is extinguished awareness is complete, because the mind of awareness is unmoving.”

“Good man! To know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages. All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, cultivating by this, are thus able to be forever free of all illusions.”

Good man! To know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means (without borrowing other methods or devices - freely, freely!); to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages. All bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, cultivating by this, are thus able to be forever free of all illusions.

To know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages” - this is the World-Honored One’s instruction on how to cultivate the samadhi of the illusory.
The Awakening of Faith says:
Be confident in your own nature, know the mind’s deluded agitation and that there is no previous realm; cultivate the method of distance
to know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages”
Because of truly knowing that there is no previous realm, by various means give rise to the practice of accordance,
without taking and without thinking
Through the power of long, distant cultivation, ignorance is then extinguished
Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise
Because of no arising
(because the mind does not arise)
, the realm accordingly passes away
Because both cause and condition entirely pass away, the marks of the mind are all exhausted; this is called attaining nirvana, accomplishing the spontaneous karma.

[Be confident in your own nature] deeply believe that one’s own nature is the Buddha. [Know the mind’s deluded agitation] know that because one’s own mind deludedly agitates, the fundamental nature transforms into the consciousness-nature and one falls to the level of a sentient being (see
Mind, Self-nature, and the Tathagata-store

). Therefore the present cultivation is to stop this agitation: without taking and without thinking. Through the power of long cultivation, one returns the consciousness-nature to its fundamental-state nature. [There is no previous realm] there is no present realm. The appearance of a realm is an illusion that appears because the mind deludedly agitates. [Both cause and condition entirely pass away] The mind’s deluded agitation is the cause for the appearing of the realm; and the appearing of the realm in turn becomes the aiding condition for the mind’s agitation, causing the mind to agitate all the more. Cause and result each support the other, growing ever stronger. “Both cause and condition entirely pass away” means the mind does not deludedly agitate, and the realm passes away as well.
Q: How, concretely, does one become free of illusion?

A: Be aware at once, see through the illusory marks, withstand the allure and the coercion of the illusory marks, extinguish the feelings of love and aversion, do not take up the marks, and remain unmoved. Master Guifeng’s Chart of the Teacher-student Succession of the Chan School of the Mind says:

“Realize that the various dharmas are like a dream; originally there is nothing at all. Mind and realm are originally still; it is not that they are now first empty. Deluded into existence, one sees the matters of flourishing and decay, noble and base. Since the marks of things exist, they contradict or accord with one another, and feelings of love and aversion arise. When feelings arise, one is bound by all the sufferings. Yet it is all dream-doing and dream-receiving - what loss or gain is there? With this wisdom that can realize, even the dream-mind too is like a dream; even suppose there were a single dharma surpassing nirvana, it too is like a dream, like an illusion. Having reached the original nothingness, it is fitting to lose the self and forsake feeling. When feeling is forsaken, the cause of suffering is cut off, and only then does one pass beyond all suffering and distress. This is to take the forsaking of feeling as the cultivation.”

(Translation: realizing that the various dharmas are like a dream, originally these do not exist; mind and realm are originally empty and still, it is not that only today they are emptied. Deluded into existence, one sees the matters of flourishing and decay, noble and base. Since the marks of things exist, realm and mind accord or contradict, and feelings of love and aversion arise. When feeling arises, one is bound by all the sufferings. Yet all this is dream-doing and dream-receiving - what loss or gain? With this wisdom that can realize, even the dream-mind too is illusion; even suppose there were a dharma surpassing nirvana, this too is illusion. Since one already penetrates the original nothingness, it is fitting to lose self (no-self) and forsake feeling. When feeling is forsaken, the cause of suffering is cut off, and only then does one pass beyond all suffering and distress. This is to take the forsaking of feeling as the cultivation.)

[Forsake feeling] to do away with feeling. In ancient texts, “forget” is used for “lose,” meaning “extinguish.” So “lose self and forsake feeling” means: lose self and destroy feeling. “This is to take the forsaking of feeling as the cultivation” means: this takes the destruction of feeling (extinguishing the feelings of love and aversion) as the cultivation.
“Then the World-Honored One, wishing to re-declare this meaning, spoke in verse:”
Then the World-Honored One, wishing to re-declare the meaning of the above instruction, spoke in verse:

“Samantabhadra, you should know: all sentient beings, from beginningless time, deludedly entering ignorance, are all established from the Tathagatas’ mind of complete enlightenment; like sky-flowers, depending on the sky they have marks. If the sky-flowers then pass away, the empty space is originally unmoving. Illusion arises from awareness; when illusion is extinguished awareness is complete, because the mind of awareness is unmoving.”

Samantabhadra, you should know: all sentient beings, from beginningless time, deludedly entering the realm of ignorance, are all established from the Tathagatas’ mind of complete enlightenment; like sky-flowers, depending on the sky they have marks. If the sky-flowers (the metaphor for the illusory realm and the illusory mind) then pass away, the empty space (the metaphor for the mind of complete enlightenment) is originally unmoving. Both the illusory realm and the illusory mind arise from the mind of complete enlightenment; when all illusions are entirely extinguished, the mind of complete enlightenment is then fully aware and complete, because the mind of awareness is unmoving (the self-nature returns from the consciousness-state to its fundamental state).

[The Tathagatas] the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. The Buddhas of the three times are: past Buddhas, present Buddhas, future Buddhas. Here the future Buddhas mean the present sentient beings. [The mind of awareness is unmoving] no thought or reflection arises; the subtle flow is forever stilled. [Subtle flow] the subtle arising and ceasing, flowing and migrating of the consciousness-mind; the mark of the alaya consciousness.

“If those bodhisattvas, and the sentient beings of the last age, always should be free of illusion, and all illusions be entirely distanced. Like fire born in wood: when the wood is exhausted the fire passes away; awareness then has no stages, and the expedient means is likewise.”

The bodhisattvas of this assembly, and the sentient beings of the last age, should always be free of illusion (“to know the illusory is to be free of it, without contriving a means; to be free of the illusory is awareness, without any stages”); all illusions are to be entirely distanced. Like fire born in wood: the wood (the metaphor for the illusory realm) is burnt up, and the fire (the metaphor for the illusory mind) also passes away. Awareness then has no stages (to be free of the illusory is awareness); the expedient means that causes all sentient beings to be forever free of all illusions is likewise.

[The expedient means is likewise] This answers the question that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva raised at the very start of this chapter: “What expedient means, progressively cultivated, cause all sentient beings to be forever free of all illusions?”

“Then Universal Eye Bodhisattva, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms together, and said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that for the bodhisattvas of this assembly, and for all the sentient beings of the last age, you will expound the progressive stages of the bodhisattvas’ cultivation - how to contemplate? how to maintain? Sentient beings, not yet awakened - what expedient means can universally awaken them?”

Then Universal Eye Bodhisattva, in the midst of the assembly, rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, circled him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and respectfully said to the Buddha: Great compassionate World-Honored One, I pray that you will expound for the bodhisattvas of this assembly, and for all the sentient beings of the last age, the progressive stages of the bodhisattvas’ cultivation - how to contemplate? how to maintain? And for sentient beings, not yet awakened, what expedient means will universally awaken them?

“World-Honored One, if these sentient beings lack the right expedient means and the right contemplation, and hear the Tathagata speak of this samadhi, their minds grow deluded and downcast, and they cannot enter into complete enlightenment. I pray you will set forth compassion, and for our sake and that of the sentient beings of the last age, provisionally speak the expedient means. Having spoken, he fell prostrate on the ground. Thus three times he begged, ending and beginning again.”

World-Honored One, if they lack the right expedient means and the right contemplation, and hear the World-Honored One speak of this samadhi of the illusory, their minds will grow deluded and downcast, and they will not be able to enter complete enlightenment. I pray the World-Honored One will greatly set forth compassion, and for our sake and that of the sentient beings of the last age, provisionally speak the expedient means. When Universal Eye Bodhisattva had finished this speech, he fell prostrate on the ground. Thus three times he begged, ending and beginning again.
[Provisionally speak the expedient means] Speaking the Dharma within the dream of ignorance, hence it is called provisional.

“Then the World-Honored One said to Universal Eye Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good man, you have been able, for the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the progressive stages of cultivation, the contemplation and the maintenance, and even to ask about the provisional, various expedient means. Listen attentively now; I shall speak it for you. At that time Universal Eye Bodhisattva, receiving the instruction with joy, and all the assembly, listened in silence.”

Then the World-Honored One said to Universal Eye Bodhisattva: Excellent! Excellent! Good man, you have been able, for the bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, to ask the Tathagata about the progressive stages of cultivation, how to contemplate, how to maintain, and even to ask about the provisional, various expedient means. Now still your minds and listen attentively; I shall preach it for you. At that time Universal Eye Bodhisattva, receiving the instruction with joy, and all the assembly, listened in silence.

Below, the World-Honored One answers Universal Eye Bodhisattva’s question of “the progressive stages of cultivation, how to contemplate, how to maintain.” The progressive stages of cultivation are: calm, insight, and practice. Calm is to have the power of leaving thoughts; this is the basis of contemplative practice (contemplation and practice). Insight is to contemplate in accord with principle and awaken (to know the illusory). Practice is, arising from the awakening, to practice and remove the habits (to be free of the illusory). The sutra below says: “One should correctly recollect (attained by contemplation), and be far from all illusions (done by practice).” Insight answers the question of “how to contemplate”; practice answers the question of “how to maintain.”

[Contemplative practice] contemplate and practice: contemplate in accord with principle and awaken (to know the illusory); arising from the awakening, practice and remove the habits (to be free of the illusory).

“Good man! Those newly-learned bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, seeking the Tathagata’s pure mind of complete enlightenment, should correctly recollect and be far from all illusions. First, relying on the Tathagata’s practice of samatha, firmly uphold the precepts, and settle the assembly.”

Good man! Those newly-learned bodhisattvas and the sentient beings of the last age, seeking the Tathagata’s pure mind of complete enlightenment, should correctly recollect and be far from all illusions. For this, first, relying on the Tathagata’s practice of samatha (cultivating calm), firmly uphold the precepts, and settle the assembly.
